title: Abstract Factory and Builder
scopeHtml: Scope: families of objects, step-by-step construction, variants, and when not to use them. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Abstract Factory: the idea
notes.html:
Abstract Factory creates a whole family of related objects through one interface, so the family always matches. Where Factory Method makes one product, Abstract Factory makes a set that must work together (a dark-theme button AND dark-theme checkbox, never a dark button with a light checkbox).

+---------------------+        +---------------+   +--------------+
| UiFactory           |        | Button        |   | Checkbox     |
+---------------------+        +---------------+   +--------------+
| + button(): Button  |        ^       ^           ^        ^
| + checkbox(): Check |      Dark    Light       Dark     Light
+---------------------+     Button  Button     Checkbox  Checkbox
     ^            ^
 DarkFactory   LightFactory

Worked example. A payments module must talk to Stripe or Razorpay. Each needs a matching Client, WebhookVerifier and RefundService. Mixing Stripe's verifier with Razorpay's client is a bug that only shows in production. One PaymentsFactory per provider makes that mix impossible.

Industry examples. javax.xml.parsers.DocumentBuilderFactory, JDBC (a driver gives matching Connection, Statement, ResultSet), Android Material theme overlays, cross-platform UI kits (Swing look-and-feel), cloud SDK region/provider bundles.

Everyday analogy. A furniture showroom set: pick "Scandinavian" and the chair, table and lamp all match.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing it up with Factory Method. Rule: one product = Factory Method; a family = Abstract Factory.
  • Giving a "family" that has no real consistency constraint.

notes.title: Abstract Factory in code: before and after
notes.html:
// BEFORE: caller assembles pieces, can mismatch them
Client c = new StripeClient(key);
WebhookVerifier v = new RazorpayVerifier(secret);   // wrong pair, compiles fine

// AFTER
interface PaymentsFactory {
    Client client();
    WebhookVerifier verifier();
    RefundService refunds();
}
class StripeFactory implements PaymentsFactory {
    public Client client()            { return new StripeClient(key); }
    public WebhookVerifier verifier() { return new StripeVerifier(secret); }
    public RefundService refunds()    { return new StripeRefunds(key); }
    // fields omitted
}
class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentsFactory f;
    CheckoutService(PaymentsFactory f) { this.f = f; }
    void pay(Order o) { f.client().charge(o); }
}
// choose once at startup
PaymentsFactory f = cfg.provider().equals("stripe") ? new StripeFactory() : new RazorpayFactory();

Kotlin variant:

interface PaymentsFactory { fun client(): Client; fun verifier(): WebhookVerifier; fun refunds(): RefundService }
class StripeFactory(private val key: String, private val secret: String) : PaymentsFactory {
    override fun client() = StripeClient(key)
    override fun verifier() = StripeVerifier(secret)
    override fun refunds() = StripeRefunds(key)
}

Decision gravity. Chosen to guarantee consistency across a family. Alternatives: one Factory Method per product (no consistency guarantee), a config object plus if. Breaks when you add a new product type (e.g. Disputes): every factory interface and every implementation must change. That is the known weakness, and it makes the interface a semi one-way door. Adding a new family is easy; adding a new product kind is hard.

Common interview traps.

  • Not stating the "new family easy, new product hard" trade-off.
  • Picking the factory at every call site instead of once at composition time.

notes.title: When NOT to use Abstract Factory
notes.html:
Skip it when you have one family or the objects are independent. Two providers that do not need matching pieces only need two Factory Methods or plain DI.

Signs of over-engineering: a factory interface with 2 methods and 1 implementation; "future providers" that nobody has scheduled; the factory interface changing every sprint.

Prefer instead: DI binding per environment (Hilt/Dagger modules, Spring profiles) where the container is the abstract factory. Many modern codebases never write one by hand.

Everyday analogy. Buying a matching dinner set is useful; buying a "set factory" for a single plate is silly.

Common interview traps.

  • Using it to model "types of X" with only one product.
  • Forgetting that DI containers already do this job.

notes.title: Builder: the idea
notes.html:
Builder constructs a complex object step by step, so you avoid constructors with a dozen parameters. It gives named, optional parameters and can validate everything at build() time.

The problem is the telescoping constructor: new Pizza("L", true, false, true, null, 2) where nobody can read what true means, and order mistakes compile silently. JavaBeans setters fix readability but leave the object half-built and mutable between calls.

+-------------------+        +--------------------+
| HttpRequest       |<-------| HttpRequest.Builder|
+-------------------+ build()+--------------------+
| - url (final)     |        | + url(String)      |
| - method (final)  |        | + header(k,v)      |
| - headers (final) |        | + timeout(ms)      |
| - timeoutMs       |        | + build()          |
+-------------------+        +--------------------+

Worked example. HttpRequest has 1 required field (url) and 6 optional. Telescoping constructors would need many overloads; the builder needs one required-arg Builder(url) plus optional chained setters, and the finished object is immutable and thread-safe.

Industry examples. StringBuilder, OkHttp Request.Builder, Retrofit Retrofit.Builder, Android AlertDialog.Builder and NotificationCompat.Builder, Lombok @Builder, Protobuf messages, java.net.http.HttpRequest.newBuilder().

Everyday analogy. Ordering a sandwich at Subway: you choose bread, filling, sauce in order, then it is handed over finished.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Builder for a class with 3 plain fields.
  • Forgetting to validate in build() (required fields, invariants).

notes.title: Builder in code: before and after
notes.html:
// BEFORE: unreadable, easy to swap args
Notification n = new Notification("Order", "Shipped", true, false, 3, null, "high");

// AFTER
public final class Notification {
    private final String title, body, priority;   // immutable
    private final boolean sound;
    private final int retries;

    private Notification(Builder b) {
        this.title = b.title; this.body = b.body; this.priority = b.priority;
        this.sound = b.sound; this.retries = b.retries;
    }
    public static Builder builder(String title, String body) { return new Builder(title, body); }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String title, body;            // required
        private String priority = "normal";          // defaults
        private boolean sound = false;
        private int retries = 0;
        private Builder(String t, String b) { title = t; body = b; }
        public Builder priority(String p) { this.priority = p; return this; }
        public Builder sound(boolean s)   { this.sound = s; return this; }
        public Builder retries(int r)     { this.retries = r; return this; }
        public Notification build() {
            if (retries < 0 || retries > 10) throw new IllegalStateException("retries 0..10");
            return new Notification(this);
        }
    }
}
Notification n = Notification.builder("Order", "Shipped").sound(true).retries(3).build();

Kotlin variant: you usually do not need a builder; named and default arguments plus copy do the job.

data class Notification(
    val title: String, val body: String,
    val priority: String = "normal", val sound: Boolean = false, val retries: Int = 0
) { init { require(retries in 0..10) { "retries 0..10" } } }

val n = Notification("Order", "Shipped", sound = true, retries = 3)

For a DSL-style builder in Kotlin, use a lambda with receiver (buildNotification { sound = true }).

Decision gravity. Chosen for readability and immutability. Alternatives: telescoping constructors, setters, static factory with a parameter object, Kotlin default args. Breaks if the builder is reused across threads (it is mutable) or if build() skips validation. Easy to introduce later because the private constructor hides the change: reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Builder that returns the same mutable object (no benefit).
  • Not mentioning thread safety: share the product, not the builder.
  • Saying Builder is always needed in Kotlin; defaults often replace it.

notes.title: Builder variants: director and step builder
notes.html:
Director (classic GoF): a class that knows the order of build steps for a recipe, and drives any builder. Useful when you build the same structure in different formats (HTML report vs PDF report).

interface ReportBuilder { void title(String t); void row(String a, String b); Object result(); }
class ReportDirector {
    Object monthly(ReportBuilder b) { b.title("Monthly"); b.row("Sales", "120"); b.row("Refunds", "4"); return b.result(); }
}

Step (fluent) builder: each step returns a different interface so the compiler forces required fields in order: builder().url("x") returns NeedsMethod, then .method("GET") returns Optional, then .build(). It prevents missing-required-field bugs at compile time at the cost of more interfaces.

Industry examples. Director-style: DocumentBuilder pipelines, compilers building ASTs. Step builder: jOOQ and some Lombok @StepBuilder forks.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing Director when asked for the everyday Builder; mention both, lead with the fluent one.
  • Adding a step builder for a 4-field class.

notes.title: Factory vs Abstract Factory vs Builder
notes.html:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder
Goal Pick which class Make a matching family Assemble one complex object
Result One product, one call Several products One product, many steps
Decided by Subclass or registry Chosen factory The caller's steps
Typical trigger if (type) chains Provider or theme switch Constructor with 6+ args

They combine: an Abstract Factory may return objects built by Builders; a Factory Method may return a pre-configured Builder.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing by name rather than by problem. Say the problem first, the pattern second.
  • Reaching for all three in a 1-hour design; one is usually enough.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Abstract Factory: one interface producing a consistent family; adding a family is easy, adding a product kind touches every factory. Skip it for one family; DI often replaces it.
  • Builder: step-by-step construction with named optional fields, validation in build(), immutable result. Kotlin default and named arguments often make it unnecessary.
  • Director and step builders exist; mention them, but lead with the fluent builder.
  • Do not share a mutable builder across threads; share the finished immutable object.
  • Pick by the problem: which class (Factory Method), matching family (Abstract Factory), complex assembly (Builder).
